Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette: Marius, a 26-year-old European fisherman living in a small harbor town, told me that his world had been shattered when he was captured by a paramilitary group during a fishing excursion. He was dragged into an abandoned warehouse, locked in a cramped concrete room, and subjected to days of psychological torture. The interrogators whispered threats, repeatedly struck him with a wooden bat, and forced him to watch live footage of other fishermen being beaten. He recalled the cold metal of the restraints against his wrists, the smell of sweat, and the relentless pounding on his chest that left him breathless and terrified. When he finally escaped, the memory of the pounding and the hiss of the guard's voice was engraved in him, and it haunted him long after the storm of violence had passed. A few weeks later, the sound of babies' cries would catch Marius off-guard while he was fishing near the pier. The high-pitch wail would immediately bring the warehouse's cramped room to the surface of his mind, the memory of the walls closing in and the guard's fingers pressed against his throat. That vivid recollection, accompanied by an intense surge of rage, would flare up in his chest, making him feel as if he were back in that claustrophobic space. The memory's sudden return would also trigger his sense of danger: he would scan the surrounding area, looking for hidden weapons, and feel an urgent need to keep his back against a wall, as if it were a shield against unseen attackers. The intensity of the recalled pain-burning aches in his shoulders and ribs-would spread across his body, matching the physical sensation he had felt in the warehouse. Thus, the auditory trigger of babies' cries had become a doorway to the memory, and the memory's fury would ignite a heightened perception of threat. Once Marius began to feel threatened, the cycle tightened. The belief that a hidden weapon could strike at any moment would make the mere sight of a fishing rod or a tool a potential danger, so he would stare at the objects in his environment with a wary eye, feeling that they might become weapons. That constant monitoring would keep his body tense and ready, and the anxiety would in turn sharpen his awareness of any sudden noise. Even the faintest creak of a boat's hull would stir memories of the guard's footsteps and the feeling of being trapped behind a wall. In turn, those memories would push Marius to seek out situations where he could align his back against a physical barrier-a dock wall, a fishing boat's bulkhead-so that he could observe his surroundings without feeling vulnerable. The sense of threat would therefore propel him back into the triggering scenarios he had been trying to avoid, creating a self-reinforcing loop that made his everyday life increasingly fraught. The cycle began to touch his work and home life. He stopped riding the local bus to reach the mainland market, because the rumble of the engine and the close proximity of strangers triggered his fear of being surrounded and monitored. He would arrive at the dock with a hastened step, clutching his fishing gear as if it were a weapon. At home, he kept his bedroom door locked, positioned his couch against the back wall, and kept a flashlight on the nightstand, always ready to flash it at the slightest disturbance. The persistent threat monitoring had also strained his marriage; his wife, Elena, grew frustrated by his sudden mood swings and his refusal to attend their children's school events, insisting that he come home early to feel safe. Marius, in turn, felt increasingly isolated and guilty, as if he were failing his family by allowing the memories to dictate his actions. When he finally reached out for help, it was after a night in which he could not sleep because the sound of distant waves had made his heart pound and his body ache in the exact spots where the guard had struck him. He realized that each time he heard a baby's cry, he was pulled back to that room and could not escape the flood of rage, pain, and fear. He feared that the cycle would destroy his livelihood, erode his marriage, and trap him forever in a state of hypervigilance. He came to the clinic hoping to break that loop, to find a way to face the sounds that now haunted him, and to regain the calm he once had in the open sea.
